FEDERAL WARN ACT: GOVERNMENT NOTICE, AGGREGATION, AND BUSINESS TRANSFER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS FEDERAL WARN ACT INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet supplements this corpus's WARN Act Layoff Notice document, which explains the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act's basic 100-employee/50-or-500-employee coverage thresholds, the 60-day notice requirement running to Jordan Lee or a union representative, the three statutory exceptions to that 60-day period, and back-pay liability for a violation. It does not restate any of that. Instead it addresses a separate set of federal WARN Act rules that document does not state: who besides affected employees must also receive notice, how notice content differs for those additional recipients, how the law counts job losses that come in smaller separate rounds, how it defines the "single site of employment" a layoff is measured against, how a sale of Acme, Inc.'s business affects who is responsible for notice, and how back-pay liability can be offset. It states general legal rules and does not determine how any of them applies to Acme, Inc.'s specific circumstances, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

NOTICE MUST ALSO GO TO A STATE DISLOCATED WORKER UNIT AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS
Federal WARN Act notice of a covered plant closing or mass layoff is not owed only to affected employees or their union representative. The statute separately requires the employer to serve the same 60-day advance notice on the state entity designated to carry out rapid-response dislocated-worker activities and on the chief elected official of the unit of local government where the closing or layoff will occur. If more than one unit of local government could receive it, the statute picks the one to which the employer pays the highest taxes for the preceding year. A Department of Labor regulation implementing this section confirms that whoever within the employer's organization is assigned to prepare notice is responsible for delivering it to all three recipient categories, not just to employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "to the State or entity designated by the State to carry out rapid response activities under section 3174(a)(2)(A) of this title , and the chief elected official of the unit of local government within which such closing or layoff is to occur."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2102(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, notice to employees, State dislocated worker units, and local governments (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2102)
  "It is the responsibility of the employer to decide the most appropriate person within the employer 's organization to prepare and deliver the notice to affected employees or their representative (s), the State dislocated worker unit and the chief elected official of a unit of local government ."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.4(a) (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation, who must give notice and to whom (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.4)
  Known gap: This clause states who must receive notice, not what happens if the state or local recipients are omitted while employees are timely notified — that consequence (a local-government civil penalty, addressed elsewhere in this document) is a separate statutory provision with its own conditions. It also does not address California's separate and more demanding Cal/WARN notice-recipient and content rules, already covered in this corpus's California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) Information Sheet, which independently apply to employers meeting Cal/WARN's own, lower coverage threshold.

THE GOVERNMENT-UNIT NOTICE MUST CONTAIN DIFFERENT INFORMATION THAN THE EMPLOYEE NOTICE
The regulation implementing the WARN Act's notice requirement sets separate content lists for each recipient. Notice to an employee representative must include the site's name and address, a company contact, whether the action is permanent or temporary, the expected date of the first separation and the schedule for further separations, and the job titles and names of affected workers. Notice to an unrepresented affected employee must be written in understandable language and state whether the action is permanent or temporary, the expected commencement and the employee's own separation date, whether bumping rights exist, and a company contact. The notice sent separately to the state dislocated worker unit and the local government's chief elected official is different again: it must state the site's name, address, and company contact; whether the action is permanent or temporary; the expected date of the first separation and the schedule; the job titles affected and the number of employees in each classification (not their individual names); whether bumping rights exist; and the name and address of each union and its chief elected officer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The notices separately provided to the State dislocated worker unit and to the chief elected official of the unit of local government are to contain: (1) The name and address of the employment site where the plant closing or mass layoff will occur, and the name and telephone number of a company official to contact for further information; (2) A statement as to whether the planned action is expected to be permanent or temporary and, if the entire plant is to be closed, a statement to that effect; (3) The expected date of the first separation, and the anticipated schedule for making separations; (4) The job titles of positions to be affected, and the number of affected employees in each job classification; (5) An indication as to whether or not bumping rights exist; (6) The name of each union representing affected employees , and the name and address of the chief elected officer of each union."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.7(e) (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation, required content of the notice to the State dislocated worker unit and local government (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.7)
  Known gap: The regulation also allows an employer to send the state and local government units an abbreviated alternative notice (site name/address, a company contact, the date of the first separation, and the number of affected employees) as long as the remaining required content is kept on site and produced on request — this clause states the full content list, not that shorter alternative or the on-site recordkeeping condition attached to using it.

SMALLER JOB LOSSES WITHIN 90 DAYS CAN BE ADDED TOGETHER TO REACH A COVERED THRESHOLD
The federal WARN Act's plant-closing and mass-layoff thresholds are ordinarily measured over any 30-day period. A separate statutory rule prevents an employer from avoiding coverage by staging job losses in smaller rounds: if two or more groups of job losses at the same single site of employment each fall under the 30-day minimum but together exceed it within any 90-day period, they are treated as a single covered plant closing or mass layoff. The employer can avoid that result only by demonstrating the separate rounds resulted from separate and distinct actions and causes and were not an attempt to evade the Act. The Department of Labor's implementing regulation directs an employer to look both 30 days and 90 days forward and backward from any planned action to determine whether this aggregation rule is triggered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "in determining whether a plant closing or mass layoff has occurred or will occur, employment losses for 2 or more groups at a single site of employment, each of which is less than the minimum number of employees specified in section 2101(a)(2) or (3) of this title but which in the aggregate exceed that minimum number, and which occur within any 90-day period shall be considered to be a plant closing or mass layoff unless the employer demonstrates that the employment losses are the result of separate and distinct actions and causes and are not an attempt by the employer to evade the requirements of this chapter."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, determinations with respect to employment loss (90-day aggregation rule) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2102)
  "Look ahead 90 days and behind 90 days to determine whether employment actions both taken and planned each of which separately is not of sufficient size to trigger WARN coverage will, in the aggregate for any 90-day period, reach the minimum numbers for a plant closing or a mass layoff and thus trigger the notice requirement. An employer is not, however, required under section 3(d) to give notice if the employer demonstrates that the separate employment losses are the result of separate and distinct actions and causes, and are not an attempt to evade the requirements of WARN."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.5(a)(1)(ii) (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation implementing the same 90-day aggregation rule as 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d), not an independent source (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.5)
  Known gap: The regulation cited alongside the statute in this clause does not add an independent legal requirement of its own; it is the Department of Labor's interpretation of the same 90-day rule Congress wrote into 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d), so the two citations are not independent sources confirming each other. Separately, this clause does not state how an employer demonstrates that separate rounds of job losses were genuinely "separate and distinct" rather than staged to evade the Act — that determination turns on facts specific to each situation this document does not resolve.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "SINGLE SITE OF EMPLOYMENT"
Both the 30-day and 90-day job-loss thresholds are measured against a "single site of employment," a term the federal WARN Act itself does not define but the Department of Labor's regulation does. A single site can be one location or a group of contiguous locations, such as a campus or facilities across the street from each other; a single building can contain multiple single sites if separate employers operate within it; and non-contiguous buildings can still count as one single site if they are in reasonable geographic proximity, serve the same purpose, and share staff and equipment. Conversely, contiguous buildings under common ownership are treated as separate single sites if they have separate management, different products, and separate workforces. For employees whose duties involve regular travel rather than a fixed workplace, the regulation assigns them to the single site that serves as their home base, from which their work is assigned, or to which they report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For workers whose primary duties require travel from point to point, who are outstationed, or whose primary duties involve work outside any of the employer 's regular employment sites (e.g., railroad workers, bus drivers, salespersons), the single site of employment to which they are assigned as their home base, from which their work is assigned, or to which they report will be the single site in which they are covered for WARN purposes."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.3(i) (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation, definition of "single site of employment" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.3)
  Known gap: This clause states the regulatory framework, not how it resolves any particular facility arrangement — the regulation itself acknowledges "truly unusual organizational situations" it says its own listed criteria do not reasonably reach, leaving that residual category to case-by-case application. It also does not state the separate rule that foreign sites of employment are not covered under the Act at all, though U.S. workers stationed there still count toward whether the employer meets the Act's 100-employee coverage threshold.

PART-TIME EMPLOYEES ARE EXCLUDED FROM THE COVERAGE AND THRESHOLD COUNTS, UNDER THEIR OWN STATUTORY DEFINITION
The federal WARN Act's employer-coverage threshold (100 or more employees) and its plant-closing and mass-layoff thresholds are all measured excluding "part-time employees," a term the statute defines on its own terms rather than by reference to how an employer classifies a job. Under the statute, a part-time employee is someone employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours a week, or someone who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the preceding 12 months — regardless of how many hours that person actually works. The Department of Labor's regulation adds that this 20-hours-a-week average is calculated over the shorter of the employee's actual tenure or the most recent 90 days, and that the category can include workers who would ordinarily be called "seasonal."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the term “ part-time employee ” means an employee who is employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours per week or who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(8) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, definition of "part-time employee" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2101)
  "The term “part-time” employee means an employee who is employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours per week or who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required, including workers who work full-time. This term may include workers who would traditionally be understood as “seasonal” employees. The period to be used for calculating whether a worker has worked “an average of fewer than 20 hours per week” is the shorter of the actual time the worker has been employed or the most recent 90 days."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.3 (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation elaborating on the same statutory "part-time employee" definition, not an independent source (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.3)
  Known gap: Excluding an employee from the threshold count under this definition does not mean that employee is excluded from receiving notice if a plant closing or mass layoff is otherwise triggered — the sale-of-business clause elsewhere in this document states a related but distinct point about which employees on a seller's payroll count for notice purposes after a sale. This clause also does not address how the 90-day lookback interacts with a newly hired part-time employee who has not yet worked 90 days, a scenario the regulation's text does not itself resolve.

SALE OF A BUSINESS: THE SELLER AND THE BUYER HAVE SEPARATE NOTICE OBLIGATIONS
When part or all of an employer's business is sold, the WARN Act splits notice responsibility at the sale's effective date rather than treating either party as excused. The seller is responsible for notice of any plant closing or mass layoff up to and including the effective date of the sale; the buyer is responsible for any plant closing or mass layoff after that date. Separately, the statute deems every person who was an employee of the seller (other than a part-time employee) as of the sale's effective date to be an employee of the buyer immediately after that date, regardless of what the sale agreement itself says about who employs them. The Department of Labor's regulation adds a practical mechanism: if the seller learns of the buyer's definite plans for a post-sale plant closing or mass layoff within 60 days of the purchase, the seller may give notice to affected employees as the buyer's agent, but the buyer remains legally responsible for notice being given even if the seller does so on its behalf.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the case of a sale of part or all of an employer ’s business, the seller shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title , up to and including the effective date of the sale. After the effective date of the sale of part or all of an employer’ s business, the purchaser shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title . Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, any person who is an employee of the seller (other than a part-time employee) as of the effective date of the sale shall be considered an employee of the purchaser immediately after the effective date of the sale."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2101(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, sale of a business — seller's and purchaser's notice responsibility, and continuity of employment (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2101)
  "The seller is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff which takes place up to and including the effective date (time) of the sale, and the buyer is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff that takes place thereafter."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 639.4(c) (Cornell LII text), Department of Labor WARN regulation, seller-as-agent mechanism for sale-of-business notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/639.4)
  Known gap: This clause states who bears the notice obligation on each side of a sale; it does not address how the 90-day aggregation rule stated elsewhere in this document applies when job losses occur on both sides of a sale date, nor does it address a stock sale that leaves the corporate employer entity unchanged (as opposed to a sale of the business's assets or operations), which the statute's own text does not separately distinguish.

AN OFFERED TRANSFER CAN KEEP A RELOCATION OR CONSOLIDATION FROM COUNTING AS A JOB LOSS
Apart from the sale-of-business rule, the WARN Act carves out a second situation where an employee affected by a relocation or consolidation of part or all of the business is not treated as having experienced an "employment loss" that could trigger notice. That happens if, before the closing or layoff, the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, or offers a transfer to any other site regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break, and the employee accepts that offer within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding subsection (a)(6), an employee may not be considered to have experienced an employment loss if the closing or layoff is the result of the relocation or consolidation of part or all of the employer’ s business and, prior to the closing or layoff— (A) the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site of employment within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment; or (B) the employer offers to transfer the employee to any other site of employment regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, and the employee accepts within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2101(b)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusion from "employment loss" for an offered qualifying transfer (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2101)
  Known gap: The statute does not define "reasonable commuting distance"; the Department of Labor's regulation says the term varies with local and industry conditions and depends on factors like road quality, available transportation, and usual travel time, and separately warns that an offer of reassignment is not a qualifying "transfer" at all if the new job amounts to a constructive discharge — a fact-specific determination this clause does not resolve for any particular offer.

BACK-PAY LIABILITY CAN BE OFFSET, AND A FEDERAL COURT CANNOT BLOCK THE CLOSING OR LAYOFF ITSELF
The federal WARN Act's back-pay and benefits liability for a notice violation is not simply added on top of whatever else the employee is paid. The statute reduces the amount an employer owes by any wages actually paid to the employee for the violation period, by any voluntary and unconditional payment the employer makes that isn't otherwise legally required, and by payments the employer makes to a third party or trustee on the employee's behalf for that period, such as health-benefit premiums or defined-contribution pension contributions. Separately, the statute makes the back-pay and civil-penalty remedies it creates the exclusive remedies for a WARN Act violation, and expressly denies a federal court the authority to issue an injunction blocking a plant closing or mass layoff, even one ordered without the required notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The amount for which an employer is liable under paragraph (1) shall be reduced by— (A) any wages paid by the employer to the employee for the period of the violation; (B) any voluntary and unconditional payment by the employer to the employee that is not required by any legal obligation; and (C) any payment by the employer to a third party or trustee (such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan) on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2104(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, statutory offsets to back-pay and benefits liability (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2104)
  "The remedies provided for in this section shall be the exclusive remedies for any violation of this chapter. Under this chapter, a Federal court shall not have authority to enjoin a plant closing or mass layoff."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2104(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusivity of remedies and bar on federal injunctive relief (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2104)
  Known gap: This clause states the statute's own offset categories and remedy structure; it does not address how a court applies the separate good-faith defense allowing it to reduce liability or a civil penalty when an employer shows it had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation, which is a distinct, discretionary determination the statute leaves to the court rather than defining with a fixed standard.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — FEDERAL WARN ACT GOVERNMENT NOTICE, AGGREGATION, AND BUSINESS TRANSFER INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet reflects the federal statutes and regulations cited above as of September 1, 2026, and does not reflect any subsequent amendment to them. It is provided for general informational purposes only, does not address California's separate Cal/WARN Act requirements or any other state or local notice law, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

_______________________________
Acme, Inc.

Date: September 1, 2026

citations.quote: In the case of a sale of part or all of an employer ’s business, the seller shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title , up to and including the effective date of the sale. After the effective date of the sale of part or all of an employer’ s business, the purchaser shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title . Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, any person who is an employee of the seller (other than a part-time employee) as of the effective date of the sale shall be considered an employee of the purchaser immediately after the effective date of the sale.

citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation, seller-as-agent mechanism for sale-of-business notice
citations.quote: The seller is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff which takes place up to and including the effective date (time) of the sale, and the buyer is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff that takes place thereafter.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states who bears the notice obligation on each side of a sale; it does not address how the 90-day aggregation rule stated elsewhere in this document applies when job losses occur on both sides of a sale date, nor does it address a stock sale that leaves the corporate employer entity unchanged (as opposed to a sale of the business's assets or operations), which the statute's own text does not separately distinguish.

expectedJSON.body: Apart from the sale-of-business rule, the WARN Act carves out a second situation where an employee affected by a relocation or consolidation of part or all of the business is not treated as having experienced an "employment loss" that could trigger notice. That happens if, before the closing or layoff, the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, or offers a transfer to any other site regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break, and the employee accepts that offer within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusion from "employment loss" for an offered qualifying transfer
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subsection (a)(6), an employee may not be considered to have experienced an employment loss if the closing or layoff is the result of the relocation or consolidation of part or all of the employer’ s business and, prior to the closing or layoff— (A) the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site of employment within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment; or (B) the employer offers to transfer the employee to any other site of employment regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, and the employee accepts within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute does not define "reasonable commuting distance"; the Department of Labor's regulation says the term varies with local and industry conditions and depends on factors like road quality, available transportation, and usual travel time, and separately warns that an offer of reassignment is not a qualifying "transfer" at all if the new job amounts to a constructive discharge — a fact-specific determination this clause does not resolve for any particular offer.

expectedJSON.body: The federal WARN Act's back-pay and benefits liability for a notice violation is not simply added on top of whatever else the employee is paid. The statute reduces the amount an employer owes by any wages actually paid to the employee for the violation period, by any voluntary and unconditional payment the employer makes that isn't otherwise legally required, and by payments the employer makes to a third party or trustee on the employee's behalf for that period, such as health-benefit premiums or defined-contribution pension contributions. Separately, the statute makes the back-pay and civil-penalty remedies it creates the exclusive remedies for a WARN Act violation, and expressly denies a federal court the authority to issue an injunction blocking a plant closing or mass layoff, even one ordered without the required notice.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, statutory offsets to back-pay and benefits liability
citations.quote: The amount for which an employer is liable under paragraph (1) shall be reduced by— (A) any wages paid by the employer to the employee for the period of the violation; (B) any voluntary and unconditional payment by the employer to the employee that is not required by any legal obligation; and (C) any payment by the employer to a third party or trustee (such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan) on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusivity of remedies and bar on federal injunctive relief
citations.quote: The remedies provided for in this section shall be the exclusive remedies for any violation of this chapter. Under this chapter, a Federal court shall not have authority to enjoin a plant closing or mass layoff.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the statute's own offset categories and remedy structure; it does not address how a court applies the separate good-faith defense allowing it to reduce liability or a civil penalty when an employer shows it had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation, which is a distinct, discretionary determination the statute leaves to the court rather than defining with a fixed standard.

It is provided for general informational purposes only, does not address California's separate Cal/WARN Act requirements or any other state or local notice law, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.
